prompts.science.phenomenon.detailed: Explain the phenomenon “[phenomenon]” for [grade or course]. Structure: what we observe, what is actually happening (at the level of particles, forces or energy where relevant), which law or principle is behind it, an everyday example, a common misconception about it.
prompts.science.phenomenon.refine: Now explain the same thing to a 10-year-old sibling, without terms.
prompts.science.phenomenon.check: I'll explain it in my own words: [explanation]. What did I miss or get wrong?
prompts.science.processes.detailed: Compare [process 1] and [process 2] for [grade or course]. Table: where it happens, inputs, outputs, whether energy is needed or released, importance for the organism or nature. Below the table: the 2 main similarities and 2 main differences, one sentence each.
prompts.science.processes.refine: Add a simple diagram in words: arrows from inputs to outputs for each process.
prompts.science.processes.check: Ask 5 questions like “does this belong to the first, the second or both?”. Check after I answer.
prompts.science.experiment.short: Help me describe an experiment for a report: [what we did]
prompts.science.experiment.detailed: Help me write up a [subject] experiment report. What we did: [what we did]. What we got: [results]. Give the structure: aim, hypothesis, equipment, method, results (how to lay out the table), conclusion. Write hints on what to put in each section, not finished text.
prompts.science.experiment.refine: My method section is too vague: [text]. Suggest what details to add so the experiment could be repeated.
prompts.science.experiment.check: Here's my conclusion: [conclusion]. Does it follow from the results, or am I claiming more than the experiment showed?
prompts.science.hypothesis.short: Help me form a hypothesis for this question: [question]
prompts.science.hypothesis.detailed: My research question: [question]. Suggest 3 hypotheses in the form “if…, then…”. For each: which variable we change, which we measure, which we keep constant, and what result would disprove it. Mark which is easiest to test in a school setting.
prompts.science.hypothesis.refine: My hypothesis is too broad: [hypothesis]. Narrow it down to something measurable in one lesson.
prompts.science.hypothesis.check: Check my hypothesis: [hypothesis]. Can it be disproved? Are the variables clearly named?
prompts.science.results.short: Explain what these experimental results mean: [results]
prompts.science.results.detailed: Experiment: [experiment]. Expected: [expectation]. Got: [results]. Help me understand: do the data support the expectation, what pattern is visible, what could explain the discrepancy (list and rate how plausible each is), what would be worth repeating or measuring differently.
prompts.science.results.refine: What's the best way to present this data: a table, or which type of graph? What should the axes say?
prompts.science.results.check: I've written an explanation of the results: [text]. Does it claim anything the data don't show?
prompts.science.terms.detailed: Make a table of terms for “[topic]”: [terms]. Columns: term, one-sentence definition, a simple example, what it's often confused with and how it differs. If the word's origin helps remember it, add that.
prompts.science.terms.refine: Connect these terms into one map: what follows from what and what is part of what.
prompts.science.terms.check: Let's do flashcards: you give a definition, I name the term. Start with the hardest.
prompts.science.causes.short: What are the causes and effects of [phenomenon]?
prompts.science.causes.detailed: Build a cause-and-effect chain for “[phenomenon]”: from the root cause to the result, step by step, with arrows. For each link give the mechanism: why one leads to the other. Separately mark links where scientists still disagree or data are limited.
prompts.science.causes.refine: What happens if we remove the link [link]? How does the chain change?
prompts.science.causes.check: Here's my chain: [chain]. Where have I skipped a step or mixed up cause and effect?
prompts.science.fact.short: What here is established fact and what is assumption? [text]
prompts.science.fact.detailed: Analyse the text: [text]. Table: claim, type (established fact, scientific hypothesis, opinion, exaggeration), what it's based on, what to check. Don't judge things you're unsure about: write “needs checking”.
prompts.science.fact.refine: For item [number], explain what research would be needed to turn the assumption into fact.
prompts.science.fact.check: I think “[claim]” is a fact. What grounds do I have and what's missing?
prompts.science.limits.short: What are the limitations of this experiment? [description]
prompts.science.limits.detailed: Here's an experiment description: [description]. Find its limitations: sample size, control of variables, instrument precision, repeatability, possible bias. For each: how it might affect the conclusion (slightly, noticeably, strongly) and how to reduce it next time.
prompts.science.limits.refine: Which limitation is the most serious? Suggest how to redesign the experiment to remove it.
prompts.science.limits.check: I've written the limitations section: [text]. Is it specific enough? What should I add?
prompts.science.demo.short: Suggest a safe demonstration for “[topic]” using household items.
prompts.science.demo.detailed: Suggest 3 safe demonstrations for “[topic]” for [grade or course]. Conditions: household items only, no fire, heating, mains electricity, sharp objects or chemicals. For each: what's needed, the steps, what should be seen, which phenomenon it shows, what could go wrong.
prompts.science.demo.refine: The demonstration didn't work: [what happened]. What could be the reasons and what should I change?
prompts.science.demo.check: Write 3 questions for classmates after the demonstration to check they understood the phenomenon.

verify.science.phenomenon: Compare the explanation with your textbook: AI may simplify a phenomenon until the explanation is no longer correct.
verify.science.processes: Check the table against your textbook: in comparisons AI sometimes attributes a feature of one process to the other.
verify.science.experiment: The AI describes the experiment from general knowledge. Take the procedure and safety rules from your lab sheet and your teacher's instructions.
verify.science.hypothesis: A good hypothesis can be tested and proven wrong. Make sure you can design an experiment with a measurable result for yours.
verify.science.results: The AI didn't see your experiment. If it blames a discrepancy on “measurement error”, check whether the error could really be that large.
verify.science.terms: Check definitions against your course textbook: different sources word them differently.
verify.science.causes: “Happens together” doesn't mean “one causes the other”. Check that there's an explained mechanism.
verify.science.fact: For disputed items, find a source: a textbook, an edited popular-science site or a review article.
verify.science.limits: Not every limitation matters equally. Ask yourself whether it could really have changed the conclusion.
verify.science.demo: Do experiments only with permission and under the supervision of a teacher or adult. Don't use fire, mains electricity, acids or unknown substances.
